claim: One-quarter of chondrichthyan species (sharks, rays, and chimaeras) are threatened according to IUCN Red List criteria.
source_text: We estimate that one-quarter are threatened according to IUCN Red List criteria due to overfishing (targeted and incidental).
evidence_reasoning: Based on systematic IUCN Red List assessment of 1,041 species conducted through 17 workshops with 300+ experts, combined with predictive modeling to account for Data Deficient species.

claim: Overfishing (both targeted and incidental) is the primary threat to chondrichthyans.
source_text: We estimate that one-quarter are threatened according to IUCN Red List criteria due to overfishing (targeted and incidental).
evidence_reasoning: Derived from threat coding in IUCN assessments where experts documented the main threats affecting each species.

claim: Large-bodied, shallow-water chondrichthyan species are at greatest risk of extinction.
source_text: Large-bodied, shallow-water species are at greatest risk and five out of the seven most threatened families are rays.
evidence_reasoning: Based on statistical modeling showing maximum body size and minimum depth as key predictors of threat status across 367 marine species.

claim: Five out of the seven most threatened chondrichthyan families are rays.
source_text: Large-bodied, shallow-water species are at greatest risk and five out of the seven most threatened families are rays.
evidence_reasoning: Direct count from family-level threat analysis presented in Figure 6 and associated text.

claim: Overall chondrichthyan extinction risk is substantially higher than for most other vertebrates.
source_text: Overall chondrichthyan extinction risk is substantially higher than for most other vertebrates, and only one-third of species are considered safe.
evidence_reasoning: Comparison of chondrichthyan threat levels (17.4% observed, 23.9% predicted threatened) with published threat levels for other vertebrate groups from Hoffmann et al., 2010.

claim: Only one-third of chondrichthyan species are considered safe (Least Concern).
source_text: Overall chondrichthyan extinction risk is substantially higher than for most other vertebrates, and only one-third of species are considered safe.
evidence_reasoning: Based on observed 23.2% Least Concern and predicted 37.4% Least Concern after accounting for Data Deficient species.

claim: Chondrichthyan population depletion has occurred throughout the world's ice-free waters.
source_text: Population depletion has occurred throughout the world's ice-free waters, but is particularly prevalent in the Indo-Pacific Biodiversity Triangle and Mediterranean Sea.
evidence_reasoning: Based on spatial analysis of threatened species distributions across global hexagonal grid cells and regional assessments.

claim: Chondrichthyan population depletion is particularly prevalent in the Indo-Pacific Biodiversity Triangle.
source_text: Population depletion has occurred throughout the world's ice-free waters, but is particularly prevalent in the Indo-Pacific Biodiversity Triangle and Mediterranean Sea.
evidence_reasoning: Spatial analysis showing 76 threatened species in this region with highest residual threat in Gulf of Thailand.

claim: Chondrichthyan population depletion is particularly prevalent in the Mediterranean Sea.
source_text: Population depletion has occurred throughout the world's ice-free waters, but is particularly prevalent in the Indo-Pacific Biodiversity Triangle and Mediterranean Sea.
evidence_reasoning: Based on spatial analysis and supported by citations to Mediterranean-specific studies (Ferretti et al., 2008; Cavanagh and Gibson, 2007).

claim: Of 1,041 assessed chondrichthyan species, 181 (17.4%) are classified as threatened.
source_text: Of the 1,041 assessed species, 181 (17.4%) are classified as threatened: 25 (2.4%) are assessed as Critically Endangered (CR), 43 (4.1%) Endangered (EN), and 113 (10.9%) Vulnerable (VU)
evidence_reasoning: Direct count from IUCN Red List assessments conducted through systematic expert workshops.

claim: 25 chondrichthyan species (2.4%) are assessed as Critically Endangered.
source_text: Of the 1,041 assessed species, 181 (17.4%) are classified as threatened: 25 (2.4%) are assessed as Critically Endangered (CR), 43 (4.1%) Endangered (EN), and 113 (10.9%) Vulnerable (VU)
evidence_reasoning: Direct count from IUCN Red List assessments.

claim: 43 chondrichthyan species (4.1%) are assessed as Endangered.
source_text: Of the 1,041 assessed species, 181 (17.4%) are classified as threatened: 25 (2.4%) are assessed as Critically Endangered (CR), 43 (4.1%) Endangered (EN), and 113 (10.9%) Vulnerable (VU)
evidence_reasoning: Direct count from IUCN Red List assessments.

claim: 113 chondrichthyan species (10.9%) are assessed as Vulnerable.
source_text: Of the 1,041 assessed species, 181 (17.4%) are classified as threatened: 25 (2.4%) are assessed as Critically Endangered (CR), 43 (4.1%) Endangered (EN), and 113 (10.9%) Vulnerable (VU)
evidence_reasoning: Direct count from IUCN Red List assessments.

claim: 132 chondrichthyan species (12.7%) are categorized as Near Threatened.
source_text: A further 132 species (12.7%) are categorized as Near Threatened (NT).
evidence_reasoning: Direct count from IUCN Red List assessments.

claim: Chondrichthyans have the lowest percentage (23.2%) of Least Concern species of all vertebrate groups.
source_text: Chondrichthyans have the lowest percentage (23.2%, n = 241 species) of Least Concern (LC) species of all vertebrate groups, including the marine taxa assessed to date
evidence_reasoning: Comparison with other vertebrate groups from Hoffmann et al., 2010 showing chondrichthyans have lowest LC percentage.

claim: Almost half (46.8%, n = 487) of chondrichthyan species are Data Deficient.
source_text: Almost half (46.8%, n = 487) are Data Deficient (DD) meaning that information is insufficient to assess their status
evidence_reasoning: Direct count from IUCN Red List assessments where insufficient data prevented threat categorization.

claim: At least 68 additional Data Deficient species are likely to be threatened based on predictive modeling.
source_text: Of the 487 DD species for which we had sufficient maximum body size (n = 396) and geographic distribution data (n = 378), we were able to predict that at least a further 68 DD species are likely to be threatened
evidence_reasoning: Predictive modeling using maximum body size and geographic distribution to estimate threat status of DD species.

claim: Accounting for Data Deficient species, at least one-quarter (24%) of chondrichthyans are threatened.
source_text: Accounting for the uncertainty in threat levels due to the number of DD species, we estimate that more than half face some elevated risk: at least one-quarter (n = 249; 24%) of chondrichthyans are threatened
evidence_reasoning: Combines observed threatened species (181) with predicted threatened DD species (68) for total estimate.

claim: Only 37% of chondrichthyan species are predicted to be Least Concern.
source_text: Only 37% are predicted to be Least Concern
evidence_reasoning: Prediction based on apportioning Data Deficient species using predictive models.

claim: One-quarter of coastal and continental shelf chondrichthyans (26.3%, n = 127 of 482) are threatened.
source_text: By habitat, one-quarter of coastal and continental shelf chondrichthyans (26.3%, n = 127 of 482) and almost half of neritic and epipelagic species (43.6%, n = 17 of 39) are threatened.
evidence_reasoning: Direct count from habitat-specific threat analysis in Table 2.

claim: Almost half of neritic and epipelagic chondrichthyan species (43.6%, n = 17 of 39) are threatened.
source_text: By habitat, one-quarter of coastal and continental shelf chondrichthyans (26.3%, n = 127 of 482) and almost half of neritic and epipelagic species (43.6%, n = 17 of 39) are threatened.
evidence_reasoning: Direct count from habitat-specific threat analysis in Table 2.

claim: Sawfishes (Pristidae) are the most threatened chondrichthyan family.
source_text: As a result of their high exposure to coastal shallow-water fisheries and their large body size, sawfishes (Pristidae) are the most threatened chondrichthyan family and arguably the most threatened family of marine fishes
evidence_reasoning: Based on family-level threat analysis showing highest proportion of threatened species in Pristidae.

claim: Sawfishes are arguably the most threatened family of marine fishes.
source_text: sawfishes (Pristidae) are the most threatened chondrichthyan family and arguably the most threatened family of marine fishes
evidence_reasoning: Comparison of Pristidae threat levels with other marine fish families, though 'arguably' indicates some uncertainty.

claim: One-third of threatened sharks and rays are subject to targeted fishing.
source_text: While one-third of threatened sharks and rays are subject to targeted fishing, some of the most threatened species (including sawfishes and large-bodied skates) have declined due to incidental capture in fisheries targeting other species.
evidence_reasoning: Based on threat coding in IUCN assessments documenting whether species are targeted or bycatch.

claim: Some of the most threatened chondrichthyan species (including sawfishes and large-bodied skates) have declined due to incidental capture (bycatch).
source_text: While one-third of threatened sharks and rays are subject to targeted fishing, some of the most threatened species (including sawfishes and large-bodied skates) have declined due to incidental capture in fisheries targeting other species.
evidence_reasoning: Based on threat assessments and supported by literature on bycatch impacts.

claim: Half of the 69 high-volume or high-value sharks and rays in the global fin trade are threatened (53.6%, n = 37).
source_text: Half of the 69 high-volume or high-value sharks and rays in the global fin trade are threatened (53.6%, n = 37)
evidence_reasoning: Cross-reference of species in fin trade (from Clarke et al. studies) with IUCN threat status.

claim: Nearly one-third of threatened sharks and rays (29.8%, n = 54 of 181) are jeopardized by habitat degradation.
source_text: In coastal, estuarine, and riverine habitats, four principal processes of habitat degradation (residential and commercial development, mangrove destruction, river engineering, and pollution) jeopardize nearly one-third of threatened sharks and rays (29.8%, n = 54 of 181
evidence_reasoning: Based on threat coding in IUCN assessments documenting habitat degradation threats.

claim: Over one-third (36.0%) of the 90 obligate and euryhaline freshwater chondrichthyans are threatened.
source_text: The combined effects of overexploitation and habitat degradation are most acute in freshwater, where over one-third (36.0%) of the 90 obligate and euryhaline freshwater chondrichthyans are threatened.
evidence_reasoning: Direct count from freshwater species threat assessments.

claim: Habitat degradation threatens 14% of sharks and rays through residential and commercial development, mangrove destruction, dam construction, and pollution.
source_text: Specifically, the degradation of coastal, estuarine and riverine habitats threatened 14% of sharks and rays: through residential and commercial development (22 species, including river sharks Glyphis spp.); mangrove destruction for shrimp farming in Southeast Asia (4 species, including Bleeker's variegated stingray Himantura undulata); dam construction and water control (8 species, including Mekong freshwater stingray Dasyatis laosensis), and pollution (20 species).
evidence_reasoning: Count of species affected by specific habitat degradation threats from IUCN assessments.

claim: Population control and persecution has contributed to the threatened status of at least 12 chondrichthyan species.
source_text: Population control of sharks, in particular due to their perceived risk to people, fishing gear, and other fisheries has contributed to the threatened status of at least 12 species
evidence_reasoning: Count from threat coding in IUCN assessments documenting persecution as a threat.

claim: The threatened status of only one chondrichthyan species (New Caledonia catshark) has been directly linked to climate change.
source_text: So far the threatened status of only one species has been directly linked to climate change (New Caledonia catshark Aulohalaelurus kanakorum
evidence_reasoning: Based on threat coding in IUCN assessment for this specific species.

claim: Maximum body size is the most important predictor of chondrichthyan extinction risk.
source_text: Maximum body size is an essential predictor of threat status, we presume because of the close relationship between body size and the intrinsic rate of population increase in sharks and rays
evidence_reasoning: Statistical modeling (Table 3, Figure 3) shows body size as strongest predictor, with mechanistic explanation supported by citations to Smith et al., 1998; Frisk et al., 2001.

claim: Shallowness of species (minimum depth limit) is an important risk factor for chondrichthyan extinction.
source_text: The shallowness of species (minimum depth limit) and the narrowness of their depth range are important risk factors
evidence_reasoning: Statistical modeling showing minimum depth as significant predictor in GLMMs (Tables 3, 9).

claim: Narrowness of depth range is an important risk factor for chondrichthyan extinction.
source_text: The shallowness of species (minimum depth limit) and the narrowness of their depth range are important risk factors
evidence_reasoning: Statistical modeling showing depth range as significant predictor in GLMMs (Tables 3, 9).

claim: Shallow species are more accessible to fishing gears, increasing their extinction risk.
source_text: We hypothesize that this is so because shallower species are more accessible to fishing gears and those with narrower depth ranges have lower likelihood that a proportion of the species distribution remains beyond fishing activity.
evidence_reasoning: Mechanistic hypothesis explaining statistical pattern, based on understanding of fishing gear accessibility.

claim: Species with narrower depth ranges have lower likelihood that part of their population remains beyond fishing activity.
source_text: We hypothesize that this is so because shallower species are more accessible to fishing gears and those with narrower depth ranges have lower likelihood that a proportion of the species distribution remains beyond fishing activity.
evidence_reasoning: Mechanistic hypothesis explaining statistical pattern of depth range as risk factor.

claim: Geographic range size (Extent of Occurrence) is largely unrelated to chondrichthyan extinction risk.
source_text: We find that geographic range (measured as Extent of Occurrence) is largely unrelated to extinction risk.
evidence_reasoning: Statistical modeling (Table 9E) shows geographic range has non-significant effect on threat probability.

claim: The lack of relationship between geographic range and extinction risk in chondrichthyans contrasts with patterns on land and in the marine fossil record.
source_text: This is in marked contrast to extinction risk patterns on land (Jones et al., 2003; Cardillo et al., 2005; Anderson et al., 2011a) and in the marine fossil record (Harnik et al., 2012a, 2012b), where small geographic range size is the principal correlate of extinction risk.
evidence_reasoning: Comparison of current findings with published patterns from terrestrial and paleontological studies.

claim: Fishing activity is now widespread throughout the world's oceans, exposing even wide-ranging species.
source_text: We suggest that this is because fishing activity is now widespread throughout the world's oceans (Swartz et al., 2010), and even species with the largest ranges are exposed and often entirely encompassed by the footprint of fishing activity.
evidence_reasoning: Explanation for lack of range-risk relationship, supported by citation to Swartz et al., 2010 on fishing footprint.

claim: Fishing has a narrow depth penetration, allowing deeper species to find refuge from exploitation.
source_text: By contrast, with a few exceptions (mainly eastern Atlantic slopes, Figure 7E), fishing has a narrow depth penetration and hence species found at greater depths can still find refuge from exploitation
evidence_reasoning: Explanation for depth as key risk factor, supported by citations to Morato et al., 2006; Lam and Sadovy de Mitcheson, 2010.

claim: The status of chondrichthyans is among the worst reported for any major vertebrate lineage, apart from amphibians.
source_text: The status of chondrichthyans is arguably among the worst reported for any major vertebrate lineage considered thus far, apart from amphibians
evidence_reasoning: Comparison with other vertebrate groups from Hoffmann et al., 2010 and Stuart et al., 2004.

claim: More than 30% of amphibians are threatened.
source_text: The percentage and absolute number of threatened amphibians is high (>30% are threatened), but a greater percentage are Least Concern (38%), and uncertainty of status is lower (32% DD) than for chondrichthyans.
evidence_reasoning: Data from cited amphibian assessments (Stuart et al., 2004; Hoffmann et al., 2010).

claim: 38% of amphibians are Least Concern.
source_text: The percentage and absolute number of threatened amphibians is high (>30% are threatened), but a greater percentage are Least Concern (38%), and uncertainty of status is lower (32% DD) than for chondrichthyans.
evidence_reasoning: Data from cited amphibian assessments.

claim: 32% of amphibians are Data Deficient.
source_text: The percentage and absolute number of threatened amphibians is high (>30% are threatened), but a greater percentage are Least Concern (38%), and uncertainty of status is lower (32% DD) than for chondrichthyans.
evidence_reasoning: Data from cited amphibian assessments.

claim: The high level of threat in freshwater chondrichthyans (36%) is consistent with intense extinction risk faced by many freshwater and estuarine species.
source_text: Our discovery of the high level of threat in freshwater chondrichthyans (36%) is consistent with the emerging picture of the intense and unmanaged extinction risk faced by many freshwater and estuarine species
evidence_reasoning: Comparison with broader freshwater biodiversity patterns from Darwall et al., 2011.

claim: The chondrichthyan threat estimate (>24%) is distinctly greater than estimates from global fisheries risk assessments for teleost fishes.
source_text: The predicted level of chondrichthyan threat (>24%) is distinctly greater than that provided by global fisheries risk assessments. These studies provide modeled estimates of the percentage of collapsed bony fish (teleost) stocks in both data-poor unassessed fisheries (18%, Costello et al., 2012) and data-rich fisheries (7–13%, Branch et al., 2011).
evidence_reasoning: Comparison of current findings with published fisheries assessments.

claim: Teleosts are generally more resilient than elasmobranchs.
source_text: This could be because teleosts are generally more resilient than elasmobranchs (Hutchings et al., 2012)
evidence_reasoning: Explanation for difference in threat levels, supported by citation to comparative life history study.

claim: Analyses of biased geographic and taxonomic samples may be underestimating risk of collapse in global fisheries.
source_text: we caution that analyses of biased geographic and taxonomic samples may be underestimating risk of collapse in global fisheries, particularly for species with less-resilient life histories.
evidence_reasoning: Cautionary interpretation about potential biases in fisheries assessments based on comparison with current findings.

claim: The median biomass of 112 shark and ray fisheries had declined by between 81% and 89% by 2009.
source_text: The median biomass relative to the biomass at Maximum Sustainable Yield (B/BMSY) of these 112 shark and ray fisheries was 0.37, making them the most overfished groups of any of the world's unassessed fisheries. Assuming BMSY occurs at 0.3 to 0.5 of unexploited biomass then the median biomass of shark and ray fisheries had declined by between 81% and 89% by 2009.
evidence_reasoning: Calculation based on data from Costello et al., 2012 with assumptions about BMSY.

claim: Sharks and rays are the most overfished groups of any of the world's unassessed fisheries.
source_text: The median biomass relative to the biomass at Maximum Sustainable Yield (B/BMSY) of these 112 shark and ray fisheries was 0.37, making them the most overfished groups of any of the world's unassessed fisheries.
evidence_reasoning: Direct statement from Costello et al., 2012 analysis.

claim: At least 28 populations of sawfishes, skates, and angel sharks are locally or regionally extinct.
source_text: While no species has been driven to global extinction—as far as we know—at least 28 populations of sawfishes, skates, and angel sharks are locally or regionally extinct
evidence_reasoning: Count from assessments and literature review (Dulvy et al., 2003; Dulvy and Forrest, 2010).

claim: No chondrichthyan species has been driven to global extinction.
source_text: While no species has been driven to global extinction—as far as we know—at least 28 populations of sawfishes, skates, and angel sharks are locally or regionally extinct
evidence_reasoning: Based on comprehensive assessment of all species, though qualified with 'as far as we know'.

claim: The Critically Endangered Pondicherry shark has not been seen since 1979.
source_text: The Critically Endangered Pondicherry shark (Carcharhinus hemiodon) is known only from 20 museum specimens that were captured in the heavily-fished inshore waters of Southeast Asia: it has not been seen since 1979
evidence_reasoning: Information from species assessment and museum records (Cavanagh et al., 2003).

claim: The Common skate is regionally extinct from much of its former geographic range in European waters.
source_text: The now ironically-named and Critically Endangered Common skate (Dipturus batis) and Common angel shark (Squatina squatina) are regionally extinct from much of their former geographic range in European waters
evidence_reasoning: Based on regional assessments and literature (Cavanagh and Gibson, 2007; Gibson et al., 2008; Iglésias et al., 2010).

claim: The Common angel shark is regionally extinct from much of its former geographic range in European waters.
source_text: The now ironically-named and Critically Endangered Common skate (Dipturus batis) and Common angel shark (Squatina squatina) are regionally extinct from much of their former geographic range in European waters
evidence_reasoning: Based on regional assessments and literature.

claim: The Largetooth sawfish is possibly extinct throughout much of the Eastern Atlantic, particularly in West Africa.
source_text: The Largetooth sawfish (Pristis pristis) and Smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata) are possibly extinct throughout much of the Eastern Atlantic, particularly in West Africa
evidence_reasoning: Based on assessments and regional studies (Robillard and Séret, 2006; Harrison and Dulvy, 2014).

claim: The Smalltooth sawfish is possibly extinct throughout much of the Eastern Atlantic, particularly in West Africa.
source_text: The Largetooth sawfish (Pristis pristis) and Smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata) are possibly extinct throughout much of the Eastern Atlantic, particularly in West Africa
evidence_reasoning: Based on assessments and regional studies.

claim: Chondrichthyans arose at least 420 million years ago.
source_text: Chondrichthyans make up one of the oldest and most ecologically diverse vertebrate lineages: they arose at least 420 million years ago and rapidly radiated out to occupy the upper tiers of aquatic food webs
evidence_reasoning: Established paleontological knowledge cited from Compagno, 1990; Kriwet et al., 2008.

claim: Chondrichthyans rapidly radiated to occupy the upper tiers of aquatic food webs.
source_text: they arose at least 420 million years ago and rapidly radiated out to occupy the upper tiers of aquatic food webs
evidence_reasoning: Established evolutionary and ecological knowledge from cited sources.

claim: Chondrichthyans play important functional roles in the top-down control of coastal and oceanic ecosystem structure and function.
source_text: Today, this group is one of the most speciose lineages of predators on earth that play important functional roles in the top-down control of coastal and oceanic ecosystem structure and function
evidence_reasoning: Ecological role supported by citations to Ferretti et al., 2010; Heithaus et al., 2012; Stevens et al., 2000.

claim: Sharks and their relatives include some of the latest maturing and slowest reproducing of all vertebrates.
source_text: Sharks and their relatives include some of the latest maturing and slowest reproducing of all vertebrates, exhibiting the longest gestation periods and some of the highest levels of maternal investment in the animal kingdom
evidence_reasoning: Life history characteristics documented in Cortés, 2000.

claim: Chondrichthyans exhibit the longest gestation periods in the animal kingdom.
source_text: exhibiting the longest gestation periods and some of the highest levels of maternal investment in the animal kingdom
evidence_reasoning: Life history characteristics documented in Cortés, 2000.

claim: Chondrichthyans exhibit some of the highest levels of maternal investment in the animal kingdom.
source_text: exhibiting the longest gestation periods and some of the highest levels of maternal investment in the animal kingdom
evidence_reasoning: Life history characteristics documented in Cortés, 2000.

claim: The extreme life histories of many chondrichthyans result in very low population growth rates.
source_text: The extreme life histories of many chondrichthyans result in very low population growth rates and weak density-dependent compensation in juvenile survival, rendering them intrinsically sensitive to elevated fishing mortality
evidence_reasoning: Population dynamics principles supported by multiple citations (Musick, 1999b; Cortés, 2002; García et al., 2008; Dulvy and Forrest, 2010).

claim: Chondrichthyans exhibit weak density-dependent compensation in juvenile survival.
source_text: The extreme life histories of many chondrichthyans result in very low population growth rates and weak density-dependent compensation in juvenile survival
evidence_reasoning: Population dynamics principle from cited literature.

claim: Chondrichthyans are intrinsically sensitive to elevated fishing mortality.
source_text: rendering them intrinsically sensitive to elevated fishing mortality
evidence_reasoning: Conclusion from life history characteristics, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Indo-Pacific Biodiversity Triangle, particularly the Gulf of Thailand, is a hotspot of greatest residual threat for chondrichthyans.
source_text: The Indo-Pacific Biodiversity Triangle, particularly the Gulf of Thailand, and the islands of Sumatra, Java, Borneo, and Sulawesi, is a hotspot of greatest residual threat especially for coastal sharks and rays with 76 threatened species
evidence_reasoning: Spatial analysis showing residual threat after controlling for species richness (Figure 9).

claim: The Gulf of Thailand large marine ecosystem has the highest threat density with 48 threatened chondrichthyans in an area of 0.36 million km².
source_text: Indeed, the Gulf of Thailand large marine ecosystem has the highest threat density with 48 threatened chondrichthyans in an area of 0.36 million km2.
evidence_reasoning: Calculation from spatial analysis of threatened species distributions.

claim: The Red Sea is a residual threat hotspot with 29 threatened pelagic and coastal species.
source_text: The Red Sea residual threat hotspot has 29 threatened pelagic and coastal species
evidence_reasoning: Count from spatial analysis (Figure 9).

claim: There are 15 irreplaceable marine hotspots that harbor all 66 threatened endemic chondrichthyan species.
source_text: There are 15 irreplaceable marine hotspots that harbor all 66 threatened endemic species
evidence_reasoning: Spatial analysis of endemism and irreplaceability (Figure 8).

claim: Throughout much of the pelagic ocean, 86% of chondrichthyan species are threatened or Near Threatened.
source_text: Throughout much of the pelagic ocean, threat is greater than expected based on species richness alone, species richness is low (n = 30) and a high percentage (86%) are threatened (n = 16) or Near Threatened (n = 10).
evidence_reasoning: Count from pelagic species assessments.

claim: Only four pelagic chondrichthyan species are of Least Concern.
source_text: Only four are of Least Concern (Salmon shark Lamna ditropis, Goblin shark Mitsukurina owstoni, Longnose pygmy Shark Heteroscymnoides marleyi, and Largetooth cookiecutter shark Isistius plutodus)
evidence_reasoning: Direct count from pelagic species assessments.

claim: Over half of chondrichthyan species are predicted to be threatened or Near Threatened (53.9%).
source_text: Over half of species are predicted to be threatened or Near Threatened (n = 561, 53.9%, Table 1).
evidence_reasoning: Sum of predicted threatened (249) and Near Threatened (312) species.

claim: Chondrichthyans have one of the highest rates of Data Deficiency of any taxon assessed to date.
source_text: A very high percentage of species are DD (46%, 487 species); that is one of the highest rates of Data Deficiency of any taxon to date
evidence_reasoning: Comparison with other taxa from Hoffmann et al., 2010.

claim: Coastal species are more exposed to the combined threats of fishing and habitat degradation than offshore species.
source_text: Coastal species are more exposed to the combined threats of fishing and habitat degradation than those offshore in pelagic and deepwater ecosystems.
evidence_reasoning: Pattern from habitat-specific threat analysis (Table 2) and spatial analysis.

claim: Coastal and continental shelf chondrichthyans greater than 1 m total length have more than 50% chance of being threatened.
source_text: Coastal and continental shelf and pelagic species greater than 1 m total length have a more than 50% chance of being threatened, compared to ∼12% risk for a similar-sized deepwater species
evidence_reasoning: Prediction from GLMM models (Figure 5, Table 9).

claim: Pelagic chondrichthyans greater than 1 m total length have more than 50% chance of being threatened.
source_text: Coastal and continental shelf and pelagic species greater than 1 m total length have a more than 50% chance of being threatened, compared to ∼12% risk for a similar-sized deepwater species
evidence_reasoning: Prediction from GLMM models (Figure 5, Table 9).

claim: Deepwater chondrichthyans of similar size (>1 m) have approximately 12% risk of being threatened.
source_text: Coastal and continental shelf and pelagic species greater than 1 m total length have a more than 50% chance of being threatened, compared to ∼12% risk for a similar-sized deepwater species
evidence_reasoning: Prediction from GLMM models (Figure 5, Table 9).

claim: Deepwater chondrichthyans are intrinsically more sensitive to overfishing than shallow-water relatives due to slow growth and lower productivity.
source_text: While deepwater chondrichthyans, due to their slow growth and lower productivity, are intrinsically more sensitive to overfishing than their shallow-water relatives (García et al., 2008; Simpfendorfer and Kyne, 2009) for a given body size they are less threatened—largely because they are inaccessible to most fisheries
evidence_reasoning: Life history principle from cited literature.

claim: Deepwater chondrichthyans are less threatened than shallow-water species of similar size because they are inaccessible to most fisheries.
source_text: for a given body size they are less threatened—largely because they are inaccessible to most fisheries
evidence_reasoning: Explanation for pattern observed in statistical models (Figure 5).

claim: Most threatened chondrichthyans (81%, n = 148 of 181) were assessed using the Red List population reduction over time Criterion A.
source_text: We assessed most threatened chondrichthyans (81%, n = 148 of 181) using the Red List population reduction over time Criterion A.
evidence_reasoning: Count from IUCN assessment criteria used.

claim: 29 threatened chondrichthyan species were assessed using the IUCN geographic range Criterion B.
source_text: The remaining threatened species were assessed using the IUCN geographic range Criterion B (n = 29)
evidence_reasoning: Count from IUCN assessment criteria used.

claim: 4 threatened chondrichthyan species were assessed using the small population size and decline Criterion C.
source_text: or the small population size and decline Criterion C (n = 4: Borneo shark Carcharhinus borneensis, Colclough's shark Brachaelurus colcloughi, Northern river shark Glyphis garricki, and Speartooth shark Glyphis glyphis).
evidence_reasoning: Count and species list from IUCN assessment criteria used.

claim: One-third of all chondrichthyan species have been described in the past thirty years.
source_text: One-third of all species have been described in the past thirty years.
evidence_reasoning: Taxonomic trend from species description records.

claim: A new chondrichthyan species has been described, on average, almost every 2–3 weeks since the 1970s.
source_text: Scientists have described a new chondrichthyan species, on average, almost every 2–3 weeks since the 1970s
evidence_reasoning: Calculation from taxonomic description records (Last, 2007; White and Last, 2012).

claim: Since 2005, scientists have recognized an additional ~140 living chondrichthyan species.
source_text: Since Leonard V J Compagno completed the global checklist in 2005, scientists have recognized an additional ∼140 species (mostly new) living chondrichthyan species.
evidence_reasoning: Count from taxonomic records since 2005 baseline.

claim: 70 previously undescribed chondrichthyan species worldwide were described in three CSIRO special publications published in 2008.
source_text: In particular, three CSIRO special publications published in 2008 included descriptions of 70 previously undescribed species worldwide
evidence_reasoning: Count from Last et al., 2008a, 2008b, 2008c publications.

claim: 21 new chondrichthyan species were described in 2006.
source_text: The number of new species described in 2006, 2007 and 2008 was 21, 23, and 81, respectively
evidence_reasoning: Count from taxonomic description records.

claim: 23 new chondrichthyan species were described in 2007.
source_text: The number of new species described in 2006, 2007 and 2008 was 21, 23, and 81, respectively
evidence_reasoning: Count from taxonomic description records.

claim: 81 new chondrichthyan species were described in 2008.
source_text: The number of new species described in 2006, 2007 and 2008 was 21, 23, and 81, respectively
evidence_reasoning: Count from taxonomic description records.

claim: All but nine of the species described in 2006-2008 occurred in the Indo–West Pacific.
source_text: with all but nine occurring in the Indo–West Pacific.
evidence_reasoning: Geographic distribution of newly described species.

claim: The IUCN Red List assessment involved 17 workshops with more than 300 experts.
source_text: We applied the Red List Categories and Criteria developed by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) (IUCN, 2004) to 1,041 species at 17 workshops involving more than 300 experts
evidence_reasoning: Description of assessment methodology and participation.

claim: 302 national, regional, and international experts from 64 countries participated in the GSRLA workshops.
source_text: In total, 302 national, regional, and international experts from 64 countries participated in the GSRLA workshops and the production of assessments.
evidence_reasoning: Count of workshop participants and countries represented (Table 8).

claim: Bans on 'finning' are the most widespread shark conservation measures.
source_text: Bans on 'finning' (slicing off a shark's fins and discarding the body at sea) are the most widespread shark conservation measures.
evidence_reasoning: Assessment of global conservation measures from review of RFMO actions.

claim: Finning bans have not significantly reduced shark mortality or risk to threatened species.
source_text: While these prohibitions, particularly those that require fins to remain attached through landing, can enhance monitoring and compliance, they have not significantly reduced shark mortality or risk to threatened species
evidence_reasoning: Evaluation of finning ban effectiveness supported by Clarke et al., 2013.

claim: Many governments lack the resources, expertise, and political will to effectively conserve sharks and rays.
source_text: With a few exceptions (e.g., Australia and USA), many governments still lack the resources, expertise, and political will necessary to effectively conserve the vast majority of shark and rays
evidence_reasoning: Assessment of global conservation capacity based on review of management measures and literature.

claim: More than 50 sharks are included in Annex I (Highly Migratory Species) of the 1982 Law of the Sea Convention.
source_text: More than 50 sharks are included in Annex I (Highly Migratory Species) of the 1982 Law of the Sea Convention
evidence_reasoning: Count from international treaty provisions.

claim: Currently only a handful of sharks enjoy species-specific protections under Regional Fishery Management Organizations.
source_text: but currently only a handful enjoy species-specific protections under the world's Regional Fishery Management Organizations
evidence_reasoning: Review of RFMO conservation measures (Table 6).

claim: The CMS Migratory Sharks Memorandum of Understanding covers only seven shark species.
source_text: The Migratory Sharks Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) adopted by the Parties to the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS) so far only covers seven sharks
evidence_reasoning: Count from CMS MoU provisions.

claim: There may be more than 150 chondrichthyans that regularly migrate across national boundaries.
source_text: yet there may be more than 150 chondrichthyans that regularly migrate across national boundaries
evidence_reasoning: Estimate from Fowler, 2012 based on species distributions and movement patterns.

claim: Only ten sharks and rays had been listed by CITES up to 2013.
source_text: Despite two decades of effort, only ten sharks and rays had been listed by the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) up to 2013
evidence_reasoning: Count from CITES listings (Vincent et al., 2014).

claim: A further seven species of shark and ray were listed by CITES in 2013.
source_text: A further seven species of shark and ray were listed by CITES in 2013
evidence_reasoning: Count from 2013 CITES meeting outcomes.

claim: Hong Kong handled around half of all shark fin imports each year from 1996 to 2001.
source_text: While fins are increasingly being exported to Mainland China where species-specific trade data is more difficult to obtain, each year (from 1996 to 2001) Hong Kong handled around half of all fin imports
evidence_reasoning: Data from Clarke et al., 2006 on global fin trade.

claim: Catches of chondrichthyans are under-reported to FAO.
source_text: However, the surveillance power of such data could be greatly improved if collected at greater taxonomic resolution. While there have been continual improvements, catches are under-reported
evidence_reasoning: Assessment of FAO data quality supported by Clarke et al., 2006.

claim: Only around one-third of reported chondrichthyan catch is reported at the species level.
source_text: and for those that are reported only around one-third is reported at the species level
evidence_reasoning: Analysis of FAO catch data taxonomic resolution (Fischer et al., 2012).

claim: The 'sharks, rays, skates, etc' FAO category comprised 45% of total reported chondrichthyan catch from 1950-2009.
source_text: The 'sharks, rays, skates, etc' FAO reported category comprised 15,684,456 tonnes of the reported catch from all countries during 1950–2009, which is a total of 45% of the total reported catch for this time period.
evidence_reasoning: Analysis of FAO FishStat database.

claim: The proportion of chondrichthyan catch in the aggregate 'sharks, rays, skates, etc' category has declined from around 50% to around 35%.
source_text: However, the proportion of catch in this category has declined from around 50% of global catch to around 35%, presumably due to better reporting of ray catch and as sharks have declined or come under stronger protection
evidence_reasoning: Temporal trend analysis of FAO catch data with hypothesized explanations.

claim: Chimaera catches represent 0.72% of total chondrichthyan catch from 1950 to 2009.
source_text: The nine chimaera categories make up a small fraction of the global catch, 249,404.5 tonnes from 1950 to 2009, representing 0.72% of the total catch.
evidence_reasoning: Analysis of FAO FishStat database.

claim: Quantitative analyses suggest five Mediterranean shark species had declined by 96% to >99.9% relative to former abundance.
source_text: Quantitative trends could be estimated for five species suggesting they had declined by 96% to >99.9% relative to their former abundance suggesting they would meet the highest IUCN Threat category of Critically Endangered
evidence_reasoning: Data from Ferretti et al., 2008 quantitative analysis.

claim: The median biomass relative to BMSY of 112 shark and ray fisheries was 0.37.
source_text: The median biomass relative to the biomass at Maximum Sustainable Yield (B/BMSY) of these 112 shark and ray fisheries was 0.37
evidence_reasoning: Data from Costello et al., 2012 fisheries analysis.

claim: An IUCN threatened category listing is triggered only once teleost fishes have been fished down to below BMSY.
source_text: Empirical analyses show that an IUCN threatened category listing is triggered only once teleost fishes (with far higher density-dependent compensation) have been fished down to below BMSY
evidence_reasoning: Findings from Dulvy et al., 2005; Porszt et al., 2012 validation studies.

claim: The Blue shark is one of the most productive of the oceanic pelagic sharks, maturing at 4–6 years of age.
source_text: The Blue shark is one of the most productive of the oceanic pelagic sharks, maturing at 4–6 years of age with an annual rate of population increase of ∼28% per year
evidence_reasoning: Life history data from Cortés, 2008; Simpfendorfer et al., 2008.

claim: The Blue shark has an annual rate of population increase of approximately 28% per year.
source_text: maturing at 4–6 years of age with an annual rate of population increase of ∼28% per year
evidence_reasoning: Population parameter from Cortés, 2008; Simpfendorfer et al., 2008.

claim: The Blue shark has an approximate BMSY at ~42% of virgin biomass.
source_text: and an approximate BMSY at ∼42% of virgin biomass, B0
evidence_reasoning: Fisheries reference point from Cortés, 2008; Simpfendorfer et al., 2008.

claim: Recent surveys of Indonesian fish markets revealed more than 20 new shark species out of approximately 130 recorded in total.
source_text: For example, recent surveys of Indonesian fish markets revealed more than 20 new species of sharks out of the approximately 130 recorded in total
evidence_reasoning: Data from White et al., 2006; Last, 2007; Ward et al., 2008.

claim: 11% of chondrichthyan landings reported to FAO over the 2000-2009 period are 'data unavailable, unobtainable'.
source_text: Therefore, 11% of chondrichthyan landings reported to the FAO over the 10-year period are 'data unavailable, unobtainable'.
evidence_reasoning: Analysis of missing data in FAO FishStat database (1,522 out of 13,990 entries).
